chunks: Ali ibn Asbat from Abu Makhlad al-Sarraj said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when Mu'tib entered and said, 'There are two men at the door.' He said, 'Bring them in.' They entered, and one of them said, 'I am a tanner; I sell leopard skins.' He said, 'Are they tanned?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

And Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abu al-Qasim al-Sa'qal said: I wrote to him asking about sword scabbards which are called 'safan', which I make from fish skins. Is it permissible to use them, even though we do not eat their flesh? He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.السَّفَنَ: A specific type of scabbard or covering
key_terms.مَدْبُوغَةٌ: Tanned (processed to be durable and pure)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sell or use tanned leopard and fish skins in Islam?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of *tanur* (tanning), establishing that the process purifies the skin of non-slaughtered animals, thereby permitting their use in trade and utility even if the animal itself is not consumed. It specifically validates the use of leopard and fish skins for items like sword scabbards, reflecting the practical legal reasoning of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) regarding common commercial goods of his time. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that tanning renders the hide pure and usable, distinct from the rules of consumption.
